newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Foreign firms fear more corruption after HK handover.
newsitem.headline: Foreign firms fear more corruption after HK handover.

text.p: Foreign companies doing business in Hong Kong cite the possibility of increased corruption as their biggest worry following the territory's handover to Chinese rule, a risk management executive said.
"The number one concern among our clients is whether Hong Kong can hold the line on corruption," said Stephen Vickers, senior managing director of Kroll Associates (Asia) Ltd.
"Clearly, corruption is endemic in the People's Republic of China despite fairly valiant efforts to have a go at reform," Vickers told Reuters in an interview last week.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Engineering and contracting firms, for example, are worried that contracts may be steered toward mainland firms even if foreign companies offer the best deal, Vickers said.

Hong Kong has a reputation as one of the least corrupt centres in Asia, thanks in part to the territory's tough anti-corruption agency, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC). The ICAC has vowed to keep Hong Kong clean after the handover.

"We hope the ICAC will be stronger and not the other way around," said Vickers, who spent 18 years in the Royal Hong Kong Police Force and commanded the force's Criminal Intelligence Bureau before joining Kroll.

The rise of triad activity in Hong Kong -- a phenomenon that Vickers said has nothing to do with the handover and everything to do with a lack of proactive action by the police -- is something that companies should be concerned about.
"Some triad societies have transcended normal criminal activity and there are now some powerful, well funded people in financial institutions leaking information," said Vickers.
"Businesses won't be worried too much about the rise of most triad societies, but they will be worried about leaks about tenders or private banking transactions," he said.
Foreign companies can be particularly vulnerable to leaks and fraud because of the way many are structured.
"In Asia, the matrix system is a nightmare," said Vickers, referring to a management style in which key decisions are made not in Asia but at head offices thousands of miles away.

Companies that have recently reorganised and feature expatriate managers who rotate posts quickly, and rely on risk management systems that "work in the West but don't work here" are particularly vulnerable to fraud, he said.
Hiring "tribes" of people that come en masse from other companies also can be a problem because such employees can have more loyalty to the tribe than to the firm, he said.
Such practices are common in tight labour markets in places such as Hong Kong.
Companies can protect themselves by recognising the risks and exercising proper due diligence when hiring.
Running a tight ship also can help firms compete on an unlevel playing field by assuring that no one outside the company knows what they are doing, he said.
Vickers said that for business, the risks associated with Hong Kong's return to China appear small, especially in the near term.
For example, "the prospect of China erupting into serious disorder and impacting Hong Kong business is extremely unlikely," he said.
Businesses nevertheless should be aware of the possibility, however remote, of serious problems, such as political distress in China or clashes between the mainland and Taiwan.
"We think Hong Kong will be a terrific place to do business for the next 50 years. But there will be problems and it is up to multinationals to police themselves better," Vickers said.
